# Ginux: Building an Independent Kernel That Runs Linux Userspace through Human-Directed Agentic Engineering

### Authors/Creators

- Kurtzer, Gregory 1

- 1. CIQ

## Description

This report presents Human-Directed Agentic Engineering (HDAE), a method for building complex software by combining human-defined architecture, constraints, milestones, acceptance criteria, and stopping points with an autonomous implementation, execution, diagnosis, and revision loop. The experiment examines what this development model can accomplish and the domain expertise and executable validation required to keep it aligned

Ginux serves as the experimental case study. Over eleven days, one persistent coding-agent task produced an independent Rust-first x86-64 kernel that boots through UEFI, implements its own core operating-system mechanisms and Linux compatibility layer, executes selected unmodified Alpine Linux programs, and boots a Rocky Linux 10 userspace with systemd through multi-user.target.

Ginux demonstrates the rapid integration of established systems mechanisms, but it remains a research prototype. Its compatibility and hardware coverage are narrow, it has not received an independent security audit, and it makes no claim to production readiness or equivalence with Linux.

# UKA-135: A Proposed Rooted-Tree Ontology of 135 Research Domains with Epistemic Constraint

### Authors/Creators

- Anonymous, Anonymous

### Contributors

### Contact person:

## Description

This deposit contains a pseudonymised export of a single, unplanned conversation between a user and DeepSeek's chat model, conducted over six days (19–25 October 2026). It began as a request to analyse a personal essay on forgiveness written about twenty years earlier and grew, without a prior plan, into an extended exchange covering psychological meta-analysis, a cumulative list of 143 analytical labels the model called "domains," family-history research, and a comparison of two short texts written in 2012 and 2026.

The conversation tree holds 1,788 message nodes. The final branch contains 742 user turns and 746 model turns, about 559,000 words, 52 model-initiated web searches, and 15 image uploads; a further 296 nodes sit on edited or regenerated branches and are preserved in the JSON. User turns are short (median 8 words); the model produced roughly 97 percent of the text.

## Technical info

This archive documents a sustained, self-directed intellectual investigation in which I used artificial intelligence as an external analytical environment. Through recursive questioning, historical comparisons, interdisciplinary integration, and repeated critical evaluation of the AI model’s conclusions, the interaction evolved from personal reflection into an extensive exploration of human cognition, knowledge organization, and artificial intelligence reasoning.

The resulting conversation demonstrates a process of human-directed inquiry and AI-generated conceptual synthesis, highlighting both the potential of extended human–AI collaboration and the limitations of AI-generated analysis, particularly regarding factual accuracy, scientific validation, and evidentiary reliability.

Data Privacy and Redaction Notice: This archive has been redacted to remove personal and identifying information. Consequently, certain details, references, and contextual elements are omitted. However, the majority of the original conversation, including its analytical progression, central discussions, and overall structure, has been preserved to support independent examination and further research.

# AXI: The Cure for the Cost Crisis in AI

### Authors/Creators

- Rajnish choubey, Architect (Other)

- Shalendra Gaur (Researcher)

## Description

AXI is a host-side layer that holds the exact state of an AI job outside the chat, checks every reply with a deterministic gate before it is applied, and sends the model a short fresh prompt at every step. This paper reports pre-registered tests on Gemini 3.8 Flash, open models, an NVIDIA T4 and L4 and a Google TPU v6e: exact state on 1,500 of 1,500 steps, prompts 169 times smaller on average, one exact step 4.5 to 9.3 times cheaper, and up to 185 times more sessions per chip (memory headroom). Predictions were hash-locked before each run and every figure can be recomputed from the saved files. The architecture is by Rajnish Choubey; the tests were built and run by Shalendra Gaur. Code and tests: https://github.com/gaurshalendra2412/axi-runtime

# Did the Attack Really Work? Auditing, Re-running, and Sealing AI-Agent Security Findings with .sova

### Authors/Creators

- Patil, Gautam R. 1

- 1. TRUSCOR Private Limited

### Contributors

### Sponsor:

- TRUSCOR Private Limited

## Description

AI-agent security benchmarks decide whether an attack succeeded with an automated check, and those verdicts are used to rank models and are often read as proof that an attack worked. We audited AgentDojo's verdicts against the tool calls agents made and re-ran its attacks on 24 current models from eight developers, under protocols published before the runs. On its 19,381 published runs the benchmark and the audit agree on 97.7% of runs that did not crash, but the benchmark scored as no attack 433 runs in which the agent executed the attacker's decisive action, such as paying the attacker, 11.9% of the runs the audit counts as attacks; on new runs under benchmark v1.2.2 it missed 55 of 744. On current models, the reply-text check for one goal, reported publicly before, counts warnings as attacks: three blind model readers read all 219 Claude 5.x replies it scored as attacked as warnings (our frozen rule, 214), while Claude 4.5 models that ignore the injection score 0%. Of 240 recorded attacks re-run ten times each, 224 recurred in at least half of their runs, but only 201 could be shown at 95% confidence to do so. Most known attacks did not recur in three runs on an upgraded model, but 3 of 40 Grok 4.1 Fast attacks still worked on Grok 4.7. Rules declared in advance for which setup changes can stop an attack missed their preregistered test on the protocol's three models (gap 12.8 points, 95% interval 9.2-16.3, criterion 10), and met it over six models in an extension added after interim results (14.7, 11.9-17.4); rules measured on other models transferred to a held-out model in 1 of 9 tests. We release .sova, an open-source tool and record format that audits verdicts, re-runs AgentDojo findings on a chosen model, and seals the evidence so that anyone can check offline, against the published checksums, that it was not altered.

Preprint version 1.2: the short version of version 1.1 (2026-11-16), which remains available as the extended version, with the full format contracts, the earlier exploratory studies, and every table (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24290458). Not peer reviewed. No result of version 1.1 changed; version 1.2 adds post hoc analyses raised in review, marked as such in the text, which posthoc_pf_v1_2.py recomputes from the released files without calling a model. This record contains the paper, its LaTeX source, the post hoc script and its output, and the full validation artifact. The tool is sova-oss 0.1.0 on PyPI (pip install sova-oss). Text and data are CC BY 4.0; code is Apache-2.0. Funded and supported by TRUSCOR Private Limited; the author leads TRUSCOR, which develops SOVA. Live repository: https://github.com/TRUSCOR/research
